A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the HERON research work. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and the equations, tables, and figures support reliable matching across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v2 reports original traffic-control simulations, APPS and MBPP code-generation evaluations, classic and robotic control experiments, and ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds HelpSteer language-model alignment evaluations, tuning-cost experiments, alpha sensitivity results, and robotics learning curves.

M1.justification: v3 adds an evaluated HERON-DPO branch that directly optimizes the policy without separately fitting an explicit reward model. Section 4.2 also changes the stated code-generation signals from all-tests-passed, percentage passed, and AST similarity to percentage passed, error type, and AST similarity. The original hierarchical elicitation and Bradley-Terry framework remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds instruction-following alignment on HelpSteer, using five annotated response attributes, substantially extending task and data coverage beyond control and code generation. Earlier coverage remains represented, including Mountain Car in the appendix ablation despite removal of its main learning curve.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 5 adds unrestricted reward engineering tuned through Bayesian optimization, extending comparison beyond the hierarchy-constrained geometric weights used in v2. Conversely, v2 Figure 6's linear and preference-ensemble comparisons for Mountain Car and Pendulum disappear; ensembles remain in the traffic comparison. CodeRL and PPOCoder remain the code-generation comparators.

E3.justification: The alignment experiment introduces Phi-2 fine-tuning and win-rate evaluation against SFT using four model judges. The tuning-cost experiment adds exact versus incomplete hierarchy knowledge and policy-evaluation budgets. Section 4.1 also expands the reported traffic baseline beta grid from 0.3–1.0 to 0.1–1.0, although v3 Appendix D.2 retains the old range; a rerun is not established.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct tuning-cost comparisons under different amounts of hierarchy knowledge and Bayesian weight optimization, plus an alpha-versus-performance ablation in Figure 4c. These extend v2's parameter sweeps and alpha reward-distribution illustrations. Existing speed-change robustness, hierarchy flexibility, and simulated-RLHF analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports t-tests with p < 0.005 for traffic comparisons and p < 0.05 for larger-K code-generation results. Standard-deviation reporting remains, but v2's explicit statement that classic-control experiments use 10 random seeds disappears. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds alignment win rates, tuning-cost and alpha results, robotics learning curves, and a Pendulum table column, while removing v2's main classic-control curves. APPS/MBPP table values and the three existing robotics columns are unchanged. In new Table 5, HERON-DPO scores 66.20, 63.02, 63.22, and 63.82 across judges; these average 64.065, inconsistent with the printed 64.57.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix J.1 newly defines F(tau) through the average decision-tree level at which a trajectory wins comparisons against other trajectories. v2 supplied a task-specific piecewise F and illustrated alpha's effects. This adds a formal definition, without adding theorems or proofs; the central mathematical objectives remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract's central claims about hierarchical reward design, performance, sample efficiency, and robustness remain. The introduction adds the specific contribution that ranking annotated response attributes enables language-model alignment. This extends the stated applications without redefining the paper's central research claim.

C2.justification: v3 attributes alignment gains to hierarchical comparisons better capturing human principles and interprets the retained signal-utilization plot as support for setting margins to standard deviations. It also adds difficulty specifying RLHF annotation instructions. Appendix M mainly restates v2's existing limitations concerning unclear rankings and equally important signals.

D1.justification: New Appendix N supplies alignment implementation information: LoRA, learning rate 5e-5, batch size 32, two training epochs, DPO beta 0.1, and evaluation instructions. Existing control and code-generation implementation details, hardware disclosures, and the code-access link are largely retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting DPO, Phi-2, HelpSteer, REINFORCE, and language-model evaluation, while removing the Bukharin et al. and Lillicrap et al. references. Its RLHF positioning now emphasizes the source of preference labels rather than requiring many annotators. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain stable.

P1.justification: The title and author line change, terminology shifts toward preference design, and several experimental passages are condensed or reorganized. The introduction's application summary and appendix headings are revised. Most existing methodological prose and the overall introduction–related work–method–experiments–discussion structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially rearranges the visual presentation: it merges the traffic evaluation and utilization plots, compresses four-panel figures into single rows, places code tables side by side, and moves the decision-tree illustration to the appendix. It removes the classic-control curves and duplicated utilization plot, adds new displays, and expands the robotics table with Pendulum.

improvement.justification: Figure 5 directly strengthens the central promise of easier reward design, which v2 supported mainly through sensitivity sweeps and discussion. Added alignment evaluation, alpha sensitivity, and significance reporting provide further support. These gains are tempered by different optimizers in the alignment comparison, the inconsistent Table 5 average, and conflicting traffic tuning ranges, limiting the overall improvement.
